source: Wu, Mao, Zhang, Xia, Dong, Cui, Wei (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought Elicits Spatial Reasoning
finding: Asking GPT-4 to draw a text grid of the state after each reasoning step beat zero-shot CoT on four spatial tasks, but only modestly on one.
numbers: GPT-4 CoT / GPT-4 w/o Viz / GPT-4V CoT / GPT-4 VoT. Route planning completing rate 37.02/37.17/33.36/40.77; success rate 9.48/10.28/5.65/14.72; next-step prediction 48.61/48.49/46.59/55.28; visual tiling 54.15/46.98/49.62/63.94; natural-language navigation 54.00/35.50/n.a./59.00. VoT vs all baselines p<0.05 (two-sample z-test) except natural-language navigation vs CoT p<0.16. Smaller models: only modest gains, mostly at low difficulty.
quote: visualizing their reasoning traces, thereby guiding subsequent reasoning steps
limits: Synthetic 2D grid worlds only; VoT outputs more tokens than CoT and token cost was not matched; visualisations often wrong; no independent replication found.
agent_relevance: Closest test of 'simulate the situation' for a text-only model: a written state-trace per step helps on spatial tasks. Candidate for a state-tracking step, not a general reasoning gain.

source: Li et al. (2025) Imagine while Reasoning in Space: Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought (MVoT)
finding: A multimodal model that generates image thoughts matched CoT on easy mazes and beat it on the harder FrozenLake, where text coordinate descriptions break down.
numbers: MVoT accuracy: Maze 92.95%, MiniBehavior 95.14%, FrozenLake 85.60%; CoT over 95% on Maze and MiniBehavior but below Direct prompting on FrozenLake; 90.80% of CoT errors on FrozenLake were wrong hole coordinates; CoT on FrozenLake fell from 0.9401 (3x3) to 0.3911 (6x6). MVoT beats Direct by 7% on FrozenLake.
limits: Fine-tuned model with a token-discrepancy loss, not a prompt; GPT-4o used only as a CoT baseline; synthetic grid tasks; MVoT is not better than CoT on two of three tasks.
agent_relevance: Visual thought helps where verbal state description is fragile. For a text-only agent the analogue is a structured state table, not an image.

source: Liu, Wei, Gu, Wu, Vosoughi, Cui, Zhou, Dai (2022) Mind's Eye: Grounded Language Model Reasoning through Simulation
finding: Feeding LMs the output of a MuJoCo physics simulation improved physical reasoning a lot; the gain comes from an external simulator, not from the LM imagining.
numbers: 39 tasks in the UTOPIA physics benchmark: +27.9% absolute zero-shot and +46.0% few-shot on average; GPT-3 1.3B with Mind's Eye 29.8% vs GPT-3 175B vanilla 29.0% zero-shot (about 100x smaller).
limits: Needs a simulator and a question-to-simulation translator; benchmark built by the authors; GPT-3-era models; no equal-token control against CoT.
agent_relevance: Evidence for 'tool simulation beats imagined simulation' on physics questions. Supports an O-step that calls an external simulator or code, not a sensory-imagery prompt.

source: Wilf, Lee, Liang, Morency (2023) Think Twice: Perspective-Taking Improves LLMs' Theory-of-Mind (SimToM)
finding: A two-stage prompt that first filters the story to what one character knows, then answers, raised false-belief accuracy for mid-sized models, not for GPT-4.
numbers: BigToM false belief: +29.5 points over 0-shot and +14.2 over 0-shot CoT for GPT-3.5-Turbo; slight decrease for GPT-4. ToMI false belief vs 0-shot CoT: +16, +19 and +47 points for Llama2-7b-chat, Llama2-13b-chat, GPT-3.5-Turbo. Single-prompt version SimToM-Single did not give the same gains.
limits: Simulation Theory of mind, not sensory or motor imagery; uses two prompts (more tokens); GPT-4 saturated; BigToM was GPT-4 generated.
agent_relevance: Perspective-taking is a simulation-style step with measured gain on weaker models. Different mechanism from perceptual simulation; do not count it as grounded-cognition evidence.

source: Bisk, Zellers, Le Bras, Gao, Choi (2020) PIQA: Reasoning about Physical Commonsense in Natural Language
finding: A physical-commonsense benchmark (choose the better of two solutions) showed a 20-point gap between 2019 text-only models and people.
numbers: Test accuracy: human 94.9, RoBERTa 355M 77.1, BERT 340M 66.8, GPT 124M 69.2, chance 50.0.
limits: 2019 snapshot; later LLMs closed most of the gap (not measured here); text-only, so it tests whether text suffices, not whether grounding helps.
agent_relevance: A standard affordance-style physical benchmark an agent could be checked on. The gap shrinks with scale, which weakens the case that grounding is required.

source: Zhang, Van Durme, Li, Stengel-Eskin (2022) Visual Commonsense in Pretrained Unimodal and Multimodal Models (ViComTe)
finding: On colour, shape, material, size and co-occurrence for over 5000 objects, multimodal models (Oscar, CLIP) beat text-only BERT, but all show reporting bias and model size did not help.
numbers: Multimodal models outperform text-only models in Spearman correlation with attribute distributions; CLIP and Oscar slightly better than BERT; model size does not improve performance; their grounded colour data correlates much better than text-only data with Paik et al. 2021 colour judgments.
limits: Small encoder models (BERT, Oscar, CLIP-B/32), not frontier LLMs; effect sizes not extracted from tables here; advantage is modest.
agent_relevance: Grounding helps a little at fixed scale for visual attributes; data, not parameters, drives it. Frontier-scale replication is missing.

source: Li, Xu, Dong, Zheng, Liu, Kong, Sun (2023) Can Language Models Understand Physical Concepts? (VEC benchmark)
finding: Scaling text LMs fixes some visual concepts but not embodied ones; vision-language models do much better on embodied concepts.
numbers: OPT-175B zero-shot 85% on material, near chance on mass; CLIP/BLIP reach human-level understanding on some embodied concepts; best CLIP-ViT-L/14 still 18.5% below humans on embodied datasets; distillation from VLMs to LMs gave a gain comparable to scaling LM parameters 134x.
limits: 2023 models; benchmark created by the authors; human comparison on sampled subsets.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for gap 5: grounding helps for embodied concepts (mass, temperature) and scale does not. Background support for an external-physics tool step.

source: Li, Nye, Andreas (2023) Emergent World Representations: Othello-GPT (ICLR 2023)
finding: Editing internal activations to change the board state changed the model's legal-move predictions as predicted, so the internal board representation is causal.
numbers: Intervening 5 layers (Ls=4): average errors 0.12 (natural set, 1000 cases) and 0.06 (unnatural set, 1000 cases) versus null-intervention baselines 2.68 and 2.59. Linear probe error never below 20% (nonlinear probes needed). Model illegal-move error 0.01%, untrained 93.29%.
limits: Synthetic game, not a perceptual concept; shows causal use of a learned world state, not of grounded sensory features.
agent_relevance: Only causal evidence found that a model uses an internal world model; says nothing yet for colour or size concepts. Gap 7 partly open.

source: Gurnee and Tegmark (2024) Language Models Represent Space and Time (ICLR 2024)
finding: Linear probes recover place coordinates and dates from Llama-2 mid-layers; the authors state probing alone does not show the model uses the direction and add only basic checks.
numbers: Probes across Llama-2 sizes and 6 datasets (world places, US, NYC, historical figures, entertainment, headlines); block-holdout and prompt-variation checks; individual space neurons and time neurons found. A one-layer 256-unit MLP probe gave minimal R2 gain over linear.
quote: this does not imply if (or how) a model actually uses the feature direction learned by the probe
limits: Mostly correlational with limited interventions; English Wikipedia only; space and time, not perceptual concepts like colour.
agent_relevance: Shows grounded-like structure in text-trained models, with no proof of behavioural use. Gap 7 stays open for perceptual concepts.

source: Wagenmakers et al. (2016) Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, and Stepper (1988)
finding: 17 labs failed to replicate the pen-in-mouth cartoon-funniness effect.
numbers: 1,894 participants in 17 labs; random-effects meta-analytic difference 0.03 rating units, 95% CI [-0.11, 0.16]; original 0.82 on a 10-point scale; 15 of 17 lab intervals excluded 0.82; Bayes factors: 17 of 17 favour the null, 13 of 17 with BF10 < 1/3.
limits: Protocol used a video camera, which the original author later argued could change the effect; Many Smiles found pen-in-mouth the weakest manipulation. Pen-in-mouth only, not facial feedback in general.
agent_relevance: Pen-in-mouth style bodily manipulations are not a safe basis for a scaffold. Closes gap 2 for the RRR.

source: Coles, Larsen, Lench (2019) A meta-analysis of the facial feedback literature
finding: Overall effect significant but small and heterogeneous; bias found for affective-judgment outcomes but not for emotional-experience outcomes.
numbers: 286 effect sizes from 138 studies; 12 moderators tested, 3 mattered; larger effect for affective judgments than emotional experience; 3 publication-bias methods found no bias for experience outcomes, bias for judgments. No bias-corrected d in the abstract.
limits: Only the Europe PMC abstract was read; a bias-corrected point estimate was not found (a thesis snippet mentioning d about .20 came from search and is unverified). Gap 4 stays open for the number.
agent_relevance: Sets the prior that embodied facial effects are small; background only.

source: Many Smiles Collaboration (2022) A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Large adversarial collaboration: facial mimicry and voluntary facial action tasks changed felt happiness, pen-in-mouth was less conclusive.
numbers: n=3,878 participants, 19 countries; mimicry and voluntary action amplified and initiated happiness; pen-in-mouth inconclusive.
limits: Paywalled: only the abstract page was read, so pooled effect sizes and moderators were NOT verified. Gap 2 half closed (RRR yes, Many Smiles numbers no).
agent_relevance: Same as d10: bodily manipulation effects exist only for strong manipulations.

source: Cai, Qi, Fan (2025) The action-sentence compatibility effect in third person action sentence comprehension (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Three experiments found ACE patterns that depend on object animacy and perspective priming; effects appeared in one direction or one axis only, and the paper itself cites instability and the Morey null.
numbers: Exp 1 (inanimate object): about 117 analysed (F df 1,116); three-way interaction of response axis x direction x sentence type significant; simple effect only for backward key press (action toward body faster), none for forward key or left-right axis. Exp 2 (personal-name object): about 115 analysed (df 1,114), ACE on left-right axis. Exp 3: agent priming gives ACE aligned with action direction, patient priming reverses it.
limits: Exact F values were split by text parsing and not read cleanly; N inferred from degrees of freedom; Chinese undergraduates; sentence sensibility task, not the original lift-off task; simple effects follow a three-way interaction.
agent_relevance: Does not rescue the motor ACE against Morey 2022: results are conditional and one-directional. Closes gap 3 with weak support only.

source: Authors per citation as Jin et al. (2025) On the nature of action-sentence compatibility effects (J Exp Psychol Learn Mem Cogn)
finding: A further series of experiments again found no robust compatibility effects and argued that effects seen elsewhere can be explained without simulating the action.
numbers: Abstract only: a series of experiments, no numbers in the abstract.
limits: Only the abstract was read; the author attribution is inferred from a citation in d13 and not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Second 2025 source (with Morey 2022) saying the motor ACE is fragile; treat motor simulation as unreliable.

source: Liu, van Paridon, Lupyan (2025) Learning about color from language (Communications Psychology)
finding: Colour-adjective associations of blind and sighted English speakers are predicted by word embeddings; the best embedding came from fiction and beat GPT-4.
numbers: Projections from embeddings predicted association ratings of blind and sighted speakers; second-order (indirect) co-occurrences carry the signal; fiction-corpus embedding outperformed GPT-4. Blind .21 vs sighted .60 (earlier line) not re-checked.
limits: Abstract read from the full-text XML; the r values cited in critique.md were not located in this pass.
agent_relevance: Text carries much colour structure for people without vision, which is why text-only models look grounded. Supports gap 8 qualitatively.

source: Anceresi, Gatti, Vecchi, Marelli, Rinaldi (2025) Visual experience modulates the sensitivity to the distributional history of words
finding: Early blind people were more sensitive to semantic neighbourhood density in an auditory lexical decision task than sighted controls, a sign they lean more on language statistics.
numbers: Reanalysis of Bottini et al. 2022: 42 participants (21 early blind, 21 sighted), blind faster for words with higher density; main effect of group F(1,39)=9.40, p=.004 (interaction statistic not extracted).
limits: Small N, Italian, reanalysis of one dataset; this is not Petilli 2024, which could not be located (search budget gone, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex rate-limited); abstract concepts not tested.
agent_relevance: Consistent with a compensation account: language statistics substitute for perception. Gap 8 (Petilli) stays open.
